Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

She told me it had started making a clacking sound during a quilt project, and then the handwheel got stiff. She said she had stopped sewing right away and unplugged it, which sounded sensible to me. I brought it home in the back seat with a folded blanket under it and the foot pedal in a grocery bag. The first thing I noticed was that the case smelled like cedar, and the bobbin cover was missing one screw. I did not plug it in before looking it over because the cord had a crack near the plug, and the needle was still threaded with blue cotton.

My first guess was that the belt had stretched, but when I took off the side cover, the belt looked fine, and the motor pulley turned without scraping. I turned the handwheel toward me, and it moved for about half a turn, then stopped. I tried again more gently and heard a small tick underneath the bed. I had the old service booklet in a drawer and found the threading picture there, but it did not show the lower mechanism. I took a photo before removing anything and put each screw in a jar lid on the table. The machine had lint packed around the feed dogs and a wad of thread caught behind the bobbin case. The throat plate had a dull scratch across one corner, but it was not bent.

My neighbor had said, “I only used the foot pedal when the light was on, and I never forced the wheel.” I believed her because the presser foot and tension dial were clean, and the machine did not have the usual marks from being dragged around. I called a repair shop in town and asked whether they could look at it. The person on the phone said their next opening was three weeks away, and they did not stock parts for that model. She suggested that I bring in the cord separately to ask if it could be replaced instead of patched. I wrapped the machine again and left it on my workbench until Saturday morning.

I did not test the pedal because I had no safe replacement cord. I brushed lint from the feed dogs with a small dry paintbrush and used tweezers to pull out the blue thread. I found two short pieces under the bobbin case and one longer loop caught near the hook. I did not put oil on the machine yet because I could not tell which points needed it. The booklet showed oiling marks for an earlier version, and I did not want to guess. I turned the wheel again after clearing the thread, and it moved farther but still stopped at the same place.

On Saturday, I took the cord and a close photo of the model label to the repair shop. The technician named Marisol looked at the cord and said, “This needs replacing, not tape, and the machine should stay unplugged until then.” She could not tell from the photo whether the hook timing had shifted, but she offered to check the mechanism if I brought the machine in. I explained that I wanted to try the basic cleaning first and asked her what to watch for. She said that a thread tail wound behind the hook could make the wheel feel locked, and that forcing it might damage a gear. She also showed me how to lift the bobbin case without pulling on the hook. I wrote the steps on the back of the shop receipt.

When I got home, I laid out a white towel so a small screw would be easier to see. I removed the needle and presser foot, then the throat plate, and found a tight loop of blue thread behind the hook. I loosened it with tweezers instead of cutting close to the metal. After that, I wiped the area with a lint-free cloth and checked that no thread was tucked under the hook race. The handwheel turned almost all the way around but caught once as the needle bar came down. I looked at the needle and saw that it was slightly bent. I put it beside the old needle so I would remember not to use it again. I did not adjust the timing because I had never done that before.

The replacement cord arrived from the shop four days later, and Marisol had included a small note saying to check that the machine was unplugged before installing it. I fitted the new cord according to the booklet and kept the pedal disconnected while I checked the handwheel. It moved smoothly through several turns, so I installed a new needle with the flat side facing the back and threaded the machine with ordinary white cotton. I followed the numbered threading path on the front and pulled the thread under the presser foot. I put a scrap of cotton fabric under the foot and turned the wheel by hand first. The needle went down and came up without catching. Then I plugged in the pedal and tested it at the slowest speed for a few seconds.

The machine ran quietly on that scrap, although the first row of stitches was uneven because the upper thread was too loose. I adjusted the tension one number at a time and tried another strip. The stitches looked balanced on both sides, and the handwheel no longer stopped at the same point. I called my neighbor and told her what I had found. She said, “That clacking started just after I changed the needle for the quilt,” so I wondered whether the bent needle and trapped thread had happened together, but I could not be certain. I returned the machine to her with the old needle taped to a card and showed her how to unplug it before cleaning around the bobbin.
